brief.prompt: Raw material, Cloudflare, 5 December 2025, all times UTC. Impact 08:47 to 09:12, about 25 minutes. Roughly 28% of all HTTP traffic Cloudflare serves was affected. Not an attack. The WAF buffers HTTP request bodies in memory for inspection; the buffer had been 128KB. To cover customers against CVE-2025-55182, a critical React Server Components vulnerability, Cloudflare began raising the buffer to 1MB, the Next.js default limit. That first change went out through the gradual deployment system. During rollout an internal WAF testing tool turned out not to support the larger buffer, so a second change disabled that tool. The tool had no effect on customer traffic, but the disable was made through the global configuration system, which does no staged rollout and reaches the entire fleet within seconds. The disable was implemented as a killswitch in the rulesets system. A rule's action can be block, log, skip, or execute, where execute triggers evaluation of a sub-ruleset. A killswitch had never before been applied to a rule with action execute. The skip was honoured, but result-processing code still dereferenced rule_result.execute, which did not exist, producing a Lua nil index error at init.lua line 314 in the FL1 proxy and HTTP 500s. The bug had sat undetected for years; the Rust reimplementation in FL2 does not have it. Affected: customers on FL1 with the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset deployed, all requests 500ing except some test endpoints such as /cdn-cgi/trace. China network traffic unaffected. 08:50 declared by automated alerts, 09:11 revert, 09:12 propagation complete. Write the public incident writeup for customers who saw 500s.

brief.prompt: Raw material, Cloudflare, 20 February 2026, all times UTC. Outage began 17:48; total duration 6 hours 7 minutes. Customers using Bring Your Own IP saw their prefixes withdrawn via BGP. Of 6,500 prefixes advertised to a given peer, 4,306 are BYOIP; about 1,100 were withdrawn between 17:56 and 18:46, roughly 25% of all BYOIP prefixes. Affected customers hit BGP path hunting: connections wander looking for a route and hang until timeout. Visitors to the one.one.one.one website got HTTP 403 with an Edge IP Restricted message; DNS resolution over 1.1.1.1, including DNS over HTTPS, kept working. Query().Get("pending_delete") returned an empty string, so the API served every BYOIP prefix, and the sub-task treated all of them as queued for deletion, removing prefixes and their dependent service bindings until an engineer killed it. The Addressing API is the authoritative source for customer IP addresses and pushes changes to the edge immediately. Staging data and mocks were insufficient; tests covered the customer self-service journey but not a task runner mutating user data with no explicit input. Write the public postmortem for BYOIP customers and network operators.

brief.prompt: Raw material: remediation plan following Cloudflare's 20 February 2026 BYOIP prefix-withdrawal outage, where a cleanup sub-task passed pending_delete with no value and deleted roughly 1,100 prefixes and their service bindings. Three workstreams. First, API schema standardization: the pending_delete flag was interpreted as a string, so neither client nor server could reason about its value; a stricter schema lets tooling validate whether a call is well formed. Second, separating operational state from configured state. Today customer configuration and operational actions hit the same authoritative database, which forces engineers to recover from database snapshots rather than reconcile desired against actual state. The plan is to snapshot what is read from the database and applied to production, then roll those snapshots out the same way binaries ship, gated by health metrics that halt a bad rollout, giving near-instant revert of individual customers or all customers to a known-good version. The stated tradeoff: during an outage customers are temporarily blocked from direct API updates, but their traffic keeps being served instead of going down. Third, a circuit breaker: monitoring that detects when changes are happening too fast or too broadly, such as bulk BGP prefix withdrawal or deletion, and halts snapshot deployment; signals from direct monitoring of customer services can also trip it. Recovery classes observed: withdrawn only, recoverable by dashboard toggle; withdrawn plus some bindings removed, partially recoverable; withdrawn plus all bindings removed, needing a global config push to every edge machine. All of this sits under Code Orange: Fail Small, whose three buckets are controlled rollouts for any network-propagated configuration change, break-glass procedures without circular dependencies, and well-defined behaviour under all failure modes. Write the remediation section for customers and internal engineering leadership.

Code Orange: Fail Small has three buckets: controlled rollouts for any configuration change propagated to the network, break-glass procedures free of circular dependencies, and reviewed and tested failure modes for all traffic-handling systems.

brief.prompt: Raw material, Cloudflare, 12 September 2025, all times UTC. The Tenant Service API went down and took much of the public API and the Cloudflare Dashboard with it, because Tenant Service sits in the API request authorization path; when authorization cannot be evaluated, requests return 5xx. Trigger: a dashboard bug. API calls were driven by a React useEffect whose dependency array contained an object recreated on every state or prop change, so React treated it as always new and the call to /organizations fired many times per render, with retries on failure. Timeline: 16:32 the buggy dashboard version ships; 17:50 a new Tenant API Service version deploys; 17:57 Tenant Service is overwhelmed and dashboard availability starts dropping; 18:17 after adding resources the API reaches 98% availability but the dashboard does not recover; 18:58 an attempt to remove erroring codepaths ships and makes API impact worse; 19:01 a temporary rate-limiting rule is published; 19:12 the changes are reverted and dashboard availability returns to 100%. Tenant Service is a Go process on Kubernetes in a subset of datacenters; responders added pods and a global rate limit. Restarting it caused every dashboard to re-authenticate at once, a thundering herd amplified by the dashboard loop. Control plane and data plane are strictly separated, so network services were unaffected and most users noticed nothing unless making config changes. Argo Rollouts, which auto-rolls-back on detected errors, had not yet been adopted for Tenant Service and would have caught the second bad update. Responders could not distinguish retries from new requests in telemetry. Write the public postmortem for dashboard and API users.

facts.value: 1.1.1.1 was globally unavailable for 62 minutes, from 21:52 to 22:54 UTC on 14 July 2025.
A 6 June release attached the 1.1.1.1 Resolver prefixes to a non-production DLS service topology; because no traffic changed, no alerts fired and the error stayed dormant for weeks.

Attaching an offline test location to that same non-production service on 14 July triggered a global configuration refresh, reducing the 1.1.1.1 topology to one offline location and withdrawing all its prefixes.
The 22:20 revert restored traffic to roughly 77% of pre-incident levels immediately.

About 23% of edge servers had had their IP bindings removed and required reconfiguration through change management, which is normally staged over hours and was deliberately accelerated after validation in test locations.
UDP, TCP and DNS-over-TLS query volume collapsed while DNS-over-HTTPS stayed mostly stable, because most DoH users reach cloudflare-dns.com, which resolves to different IP addresses.
Tata Communications India (AS4755) began advertising 1.1.1.0/24 at 21:54, visible only because Cloudflare had withdrawn the prefix; it was not a cause of the outage.
The legacy addressing system hard-codes explicit data center location lists per prefix and pushes updates to every data center at once, with no canary stage, even when peer-reviewed.
Because nearly all Cloudflare services are announced via anycast, a fault in advertising that address space produces a global rather than regional outage.
Cloudflare will deprecate the legacy addressing components in favour of topologies that do not hard-code IPs and that support progressive, health-mediated deployment with rollback.

brief.prompt: Raw material, Cloudflare, 21 August 2025, all times UTC. A single customer began requesting large volumes of cached objects from AWS us-east-1 at about 16:27, and the response traffic doubled total Cloudflare-to-AWS traffic, saturating every direct peering link between the two networks. At 16:37 AWS started withdrawing BGP advertisements on congested private network interconnects to shed load; that steered traffic onto peering links reached through an offsite interconnection switch, which then also saturated. Two pre-existing conditions made it worse: one direct peering link was running at half capacity due to an earlier failure, and the Data Center Interconnect to the offsite switch was already due for a capacity upgrade. 16:44 the network team is alerted to congestion in Ashburn (IAD); 16:45 responders find that uncongested paths no longer carry AWS prefixes because of the withdrawals; 17:22 dropped traffic increases; 17:45 a customer-impact incident is raised; 19:05 rate-limiting the customer reduces congestion; 19:27 traffic engineering fully resolves congestion; 19:45 AWS begins reverting withdrawals; 20:07 AWS finishes normalizing announcements over IAD PNIs; 20:18 impact ends. Router queues grew and edge routers dropped high-priority packets throughout. Customers saw latency, timeouts and low throughput; the share of synthetic origin requests missing the latency SLO tracked the packet drops. Latency recovered after drops because both sides were renormalizing prefix advertisements. Regional only; global Cloudflare services were unaffected. Not an attack, not a BGP hijack. Write the public postmortem for customers with origins in AWS us-east-1.

facts.value: One customer's surge of cache-object requests from AWS us-east-1 doubled total Cloudflare-to-AWS traffic and saturated all direct peering links, starting about 16:27 UTC.
AWS withdrew BGP advertisements on congested PNIs at 16:37 to shed load, which pushed traffic onto offsite-switch peering links that then saturated too.
One direct peering link was already running at half capacity because of a pre-existing failure.
The Data Center Interconnect linking Cloudflare's edge routers to the offsite switch was already due for a capacity upgrade.
By 16:45 responders could not shift traffic to uncongested paths, because AWS's withdrawals had removed its prefixes from exactly those paths.
Rate-limiting the single customer at 19:05 reduced congestion and traffic engineering fully resolved it at 19:27; AWS reverted withdrawals from 19:45 and finished at 20:07.
Impact began at 16:27, was substantially reduced by 19:38, and intermittent latency continued until 20:18 UTC.
Congestion grew router queues until Ashburn edge routers dropped even high-priority packets, producing latency, timeouts and low throughput to origins.
Packet drops resolved before customer latency did, because Cloudflare and AWS were still renormalizing the prefix advertisements each had adjusted.
The event was regional, confined to traffic between Cloudflare and AWS us-east-1; global Cloudflare services were unaffected, and it was congestion rather than an attack or BGP hijack.

Short term: selective deprioritization of a customer congesting the network, expedited DCI upgrades, and coordination with AWS on BGP traffic engineering. Long term: a per-customer network resource budget that prevents one customer degrading others, with automation replacing the manual actions used here.
